t: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into a palace after seeing Nicolas Fouquet's Vaux-le-Vicomte in 1661, recruiting its architect, painter and garden designer, and the court lived at Versailles from 1682 until 6 October 1789.

Louis XIV made the palace the de facto capital of France by 1687, drawing the nobility there to seek prestige and royal patronage within a strict court etiquette, which eroded their provincial power bases.

The Revolution emptied the palace and sold its contents in seventeen thousand lots; Louis Philippe I made it a history museum, and restoration since 1892 has aimed to bring it back to its state in 1789.
dyk: Louis XIV's eight-foot-high silver throne in the Salon of Apollo was melted down in 1689 to help pay the costs of an expensive war, and was replaced by a more modest throne of gilded wood.
ev: Louis XIII built a modest brick-and-stone hunting lodge at Versailles
Louis XIV decided to make Versailles a full-scale residence and began encasing his father's château in Le Vau's enveloppe
The king, the court and the government settled at Versailles
The Women's March on Versailles forced the royal family to return to Paris, and the palace was closed
The Convention ordered the royal property in the palace sold at auction, a sale that ran until 1794
Louis Philippe I inaugurated the Museum of the History of France in the palace
The Treaty of Versailles, ending the First World War, was signed in the Hall of Mirrors
The Grand Versailles restoration project began with the replanting of the gardens

f.made: Begun as a hunting lodge for Louis XIII; expanded for Louis XIV by the architects Louis Le Vau, François d'Orbay and Jules Hardouin-Mansart, the painter Charles Le Brun and the garden designer André Le Nôtre, under the direction of Jean-Baptiste Colbert
f.form: A château of courtyards and wings with a façade 402 metres long, about 63,154 square metres in area and roughly 2,300 rooms, set in a park of 815 hectares today, 93 of them formal gardens
f.where: In the commune of Versailles in the Yvelines department, about 16 kilometres south-west of Paris; owned by the French state, and housing the National Museum of the History of France
f.known: the Hall of Mirrors with its 578 mirrors; the State Apartments of the king and queen; the Royal Chapel and Royal Opera; the formal gardens of Le Nôtre; the Grand and Petit Trianon; the Queen's Hamlet; the court of Louis XIV; the treaties and proclamations signed there
